Although Humira sales fell 36% to $756 million in Q2 2026, AbbVie still grew 10.2% on the strength of Skyrizi and Rinvoq, while ABBVx can now be bought from Rp11,000 on Pintu, leaving the question of whether this stock remains attractive near its record high, with the next patent challenge already waiting. AbbVie was created in 2013 as a spin-off from Abbott Laboratories, carrying with it the research-based pharmaceutical division and one asset that dominated everything else: Humira, an injectable treatment for autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. At its peak Humira was the highest-selling drug in the world, and that dependence made AbbVie an example of patent-related risk, the situation in which a drug’s patent protection expires and competitors are free to sell copies at far lower prices. That cliff arrived in the United States in 2023, and the result is now fully visible. Humira booked $756 million in the second quarter of 2026, down 35.9% year on year (AbbVie Investor Relations). Total company revenue in the same quarter nevertheless rose 10.2% to $16.99 billion, because AbbVie had already prepared for it. ABBV closed at $262.51 on 16 September 2026, down slightly by 0.20% on the day (StockAnalysis). Its 52-week range runs from $190.75 to $267.47, meaning the stock is up around 38% from its floor and sits about 2% below its peak. The price change across the full 52 weeks is recorded at plus 20.63%. That position matters when read alongside analyst targets. The consensus among 31 analysts sits at $277.31, only 5.64% above the current price, and that is the lowest figure among the large pharmaceutical stocks discussed here. The reason is simple: the price has already caught up with their targets. The stock is no longer cheap in the sense of being “overlooked by the market”, and the case for buying it has to come from future growth rather than from a discount that has yet to close. Its five-year beta is 0.28, far below the market average. Historically the stock moves far more calmly than the index, which is consistent with the profile of a large dividend-paying pharmaceutical company. StockInvest.us assigned a buy candidate status as of 15 September 2026, after five consecutive days of gains accompanied by rising volume. Both the short-term and long-term moving averages give buy signals, with the short-term average sitting above the long-term one. The nearest support levels are $256.14 and $255.63, with a volume accumulation area at $253.35. The nearest resistance is very tight, at $263.20 on a volume accumulation basis and $264.56 at the Fibonacci level, so short-term room to move higher is thin. The MACD indicator still gives a sell signal, pointing in the opposite direction to its moving averages. Average daily volatility is 2.14%. Technical data as of 18 September 2026. It changes daily and is not a price prediction. Check a real-time chart before making any decision. The second quarter of 2026 ended on 30 June 2026 and was reported on 31 July 2026. Total revenue reached $16.99 billion, up 10.2% year on year, in the same year that its former flagship drug lost a third of its sales (AbbVie Investor Relations). The support came from immunology. Skyrizi booked $5.505 billion with growth of 24.4%, and Rinvoq $2.525 billion with growth of 24.5%. Skyrizi alone, in a single quarter, booked more than seven times Humira’s sales in that same quarter. A replacement that fast is rare in the pharmaceutical industry, because most companies that lose their flagship drug spend years with shrinking revenue before finding a successor. A single drug now supports nearly a third of AbbVie’s revenue, and that concentration is both a strength and a vulnerability at the same time. Outside immunology, oncology declined 1.5% and aesthetics was essentially flat with growth of 0.3%, reflecting consumer demand for aesthetic procedures that has yet to recover. Those two segments contribute around 17% of revenue and are currently not adding to growth. AbbVie’s trailing P/E is 74, a figure that looks expensive if we consider that single indicator alone. Its forward P/E, however, is only 17.30, because earnings under GAAP accounting standards over the last 12 months have been heavily depressed by the amortisation of intangible assets and research costs from its series of acquisitions, particularly Allergan and ImmunoGen (StockAnalysis). P/E (price to earnings) is the share price divided by earnings per share. The trailing version uses earnings from the last 12 months, while the forward version uses estimated earnings for the year ahead. The gap is visible in two lines of the same earnings statement. Operating profit over the last 12 months reached $22.89 billion, while net profit was only $6.27 billion. Compare this with the three closest pharmaceutical giants. With a forward P/E of 17.30 against Johnson & Johnson at 23.82, the market is applying a “discount” of around 27% to AbbVie relative to a large pharmaceutical company that is in fact growing more slowly. AbbVie’s revenue rose 10.39% over the last 12 months, compared with 8.1% for Johnson & Johnson. That “discount” is not a mispricing. It is the price the market has set for the next patent cliff, which is discussed in the catalyst section. AbbVie’s balance sheet looks alarming when read by the usual rules. Shareholders’ equity is minus $5.89 billion, meaning total liabilities exceed total assets on the books. Total debt stands at $70.89 billion against cash of $6.57 billion, putting net debt at $64.32 billion (StockAnalysis). The price to book and return on equity ratios cannot even be calculated, because the denominator is negative. AbbVie bought Allergan for around $63 billion in 2020 and has continued acquiring since then. Purchases of this kind are recorded as intangible assets that are then amortised off the books over many years, while the debt used to finance them remains fully recorded, so book value shrinks faster than the debt does. The more relevant figure is the ability to pay. Its operating margin is 35.56% with an EV/EBITDA ratio of 17.17 times, meaning its operating cash flow is large and stable. That is what supports the dividend of $6.92 per share, or a yield of 2.64%, and AbbVie is recorded as having raised its dividend for 54 consecutive years when counted together with Abbott’s history before the separation. The payout ratio of 195.5% that appears in stock screeners is calculated against the depressed GAAP earnings described above. Against the midpoint of 2026 adjusted earnings per share (adjusted EPS) guidance of $13.97, the ratio is around 50%, and that second figure is the one management uses. AbbVie completed its acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics on 3 September 2026, valued at $10.9 billion or $135.11 per share in cash (AbbVie). The target was not a product already on the market, but two drug candidates still in development. The first candidate is zumilokibart (APG777), an IL-13 targeting monoclonal antibody for atopic dermatitis, which in phase 2 trials showed around 67% of patients achieving significant skin clearance within 16 weeks. The second candidate is APG273, a combination of zumilokibart with the TSLP inhibiting antibody APG333, developed for asthma with the potential for quarterly or twice-yearly dosing. A dosing interval that long is a genuine commercial advantage in the injectable drug category, because patients find it easier to stay on a treatment taken infrequently. Chairman and CEO Robert A. Michael said the aim is to accelerate these programmes using AbbVie’s development, regulatory, and commercial capabilities. AbbVie estimates the acquisition will dilute adjusted EPS by $0.14 in 2026 and by around $0.46 in 2027, and will only start adding to earnings from 2032. That means you are paying $10.9 billion today for assets that, by the company’s own account, will not be profitable for another six years. Biosimilar Humira: the 36% decline was not a surprise and management described it as in line with expectations. Its base is now small, however, at $756 million per quarter, so further declines will have an increasingly thin impact on the company total. The heaviest part of this pressure has passed. Aesthetic demand: this segment grew 0.3% and depends entirely on discretionary consumer spending for procedures paid out of pocket rather than by insurance. Cosmetic Botox and fillers are the kind of expense deferred first when the economy weakens, and the segment has no patent protection to fall back on against pricing pressure. In September 2025, AbbVie settled patent disputes with Sandoz, Hetero Labs, Aurobindo Pharma, Intas Pharmaceuticals, and Sun Pharmaceuticals, extending Rinvoq’s exclusivity in the United States to April 2037, up from a previous estimate of 2033 (Fierce Pharma). Skyrizi has not received the same treatment. Its composition of matter patent is scheduled to expire in 2033, and as of the time of writing no similar settlement has been announced (Fierce Pharma). The year a patent expires is not the year biosimilars enter the market. Humira’s composition of matter patent in the United States expired in 2016, but its biosimilars were not genuinely sold until 2023, because AbbVie protected the drug with dozens of other patents and settled lawsuits one by one. The same pattern could repeat for Skyrizi. title: No falling back: B.C. establishes new time zone abbreviation - Daily Hive
content: It was announced earlier this year that B.C. was going to move to permanent daylight time to stop switching the clocks for daylight saving time; now there’s a new time zone code. The B.C. Ministry of Citizens’ Services announced the changes today. B.C. eliminated the twice-a-year change in March 2026, and today it announced that it will be using PCT as the abbreviation for the year-round time zone code. The ministry is advising residents that they can either use Pacific Time or PCT when referencing the year-round time standard. Ordinarily, when Nov. 1 rolls around, the clocks roll back one hour, granting residents an extra hour of sleep. That will not happen this year. “Improved overall health, reduced disruptions for families, simplified scheduling and an extra hour of evening light during the winter months are clear benefits of a year-round time zone,” said Diana Gibson, the minister of citizens’ services, in a statement. “In March, Premier Eby announced B.C.’s last ‘spring forward’ time change to Pacific Time and the three-letter abbreviation PCT aligns with how other provinces abbreviate their time zones,” Gibson added. The ministry noted other benefits residents may see, including fewer sleep disruptions, the increased light allowing more leisure time, and participation in outdoor activities and consumer activity. It also states there will be reduced administrative burden for small businesses and service providers “who may require less system reprogramming.” The ministry adds that existing local mountain time arrangements in parts of northern and southeastern B.C. are not changed by the transition to PCT. Codes like PCT are used in operational and communications systems, and B.C. says that using PCT aligns with Canadian and international time zone naming conventions. You can read more about the changes on the B.C. government’s website. Proposed changes to adopting year-round Daylight Saving Time date back to 2019, when a survey saw over 220,000 participate, with 93 per cent in support. It was late B.C. Premier John Horgan, who first proposed the idea. For the longest time, B.C. government officials stated that they were waiting for movement from our neighbours across the border so that the changes could be done in alignment. Eby’s announcement in March signalled that the wait for the States was over. “This decision isn’t just about clocks. It’s about making life easier for families, reducing disruptions for businesses and supporting a stable, thriving economy. I am hopeful that our American neighbours will soon join us in ending disruptive time changes,” Eby said. “We have heard the overwhelming majority of people in B.C. who want to end the back-and-forth of seasonal time changes,” Niki Sharma, attorney general and deputy premier of B.C., said at the time of the announcement in March. title: What Happens To AbbVie Stock If SKYRIZI Slows Down? - Trefis
content: AbbVie (ABBV) is trading within about one percent of its 52-week high after gaining roughly 24% over the past year, well ahead of the S&P 500. That price rests on two drugs, SKYRIZI above all, growing faster than 20% year over year while the company’s older medicines shrink. The biggest risk to the stock makes no noise. It is the chance that this engine slows while the price assumes it cannot. In the quarter ended June 2026, AbbVie took in nearly $17 billion of revenue. SKYRIZI, its treatment for psoriasis and Crohn’s disease, was $5.5 billion of that, about a third of the whole company. It grew 24% on an operational basis. RINVOQ, its other big immunology drug, and the neuroscience business grew at a similar pace. Other parts of the business went the other way. HUMIRA fell 36%, also on an operational basis, under biosimilar competition, and both oncology and aesthetics shrank. SKYRIZI, RINVOQ and the neuroscience business drive the company’s growth now, and SKYRIZI is by far the largest of the growers, so what could slow SKYRIZI is the question that matters. The first threat is on the market: a new oral psoriasis drug launched in March. Management says it has not dented SKYRIZI so far: the newcomer draws most of its patients from the two other oral treatments, and SKYRIZI’s new and switching patient starts have grown since the launch. That is the company’s own tracking, and it covers only a few months. The second threat comes every year, when payers negotiate price. Management calls immunology a volume business in which payers take low-single-digit concessions on price and rebates, and says the latest round has so far run like past ones. The third threat carries dates. SKYRIZI’s composition of matter patent runs to 2033 and its regulatory data protection to 2031, though the company says later patents, granted and pending, run into the mid-2030s and later. The company is already buying for the years after that: its acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics adds immunology assets the CEO calls a source of growth for the 2030s and beyond. More than the lost sales would explain, because the price already assumes the engine keeps running. Inside the past year’s run, the stock’s largest fall was about 17% from peak to trough. The options market is not calm: implied volatility sits in the 73rd percentile of its one-year range, a larger expected move than usual. A slowdown in SKYRIZI would not arrive as an event. It would show up as a growth rate a few points lower than the quarter before, while the older drugs keep shrinking. The risk is real, and it is slow. Two checks are dated. The FDA is due to rule in the fall of 2026 on a subcutaneous induction dose of SKYRIZI for Crohn’s disease, which management expects to lift growth from early 2027. AbbVie’s report for the quarter ending September 2026 will show whether SKYRIZI is still growing above 20%. Until those catalysts lands, check how large a move the options market is pricing; this close to a 52-week high, the swing runs both ways. A threat like the one above is a footnote for a diversified holder and a headline for a concentrated one. Concentration tends to arrive by accident rather than by decision.
